newsitem.title: FRANCE: Complacent French market could face shock-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Complacent French market could face shock-analysts.

text.p: French financial markets are far too complacent about the likelihood of a win for the centre-right coalition in a May 25/June 1 election and a change of government could spark a blowout, analysts said on Tuesday.

Despite a string of opinion polls showing the opposition Socialists and Communists are gaining ground on the ruling coalition, domestic investors appear steadfast in their belief Prime Minister Alain Juppe's government will retain power.

Analysts said besides the domestic complacency there was also a benign neglect of the risks by non-resident investors, fueled partly by the fact the recent Labour victory in Britain was taken so well in financial circles.
"Domestics do not believe the Socialists could win and foreigners have not really understood that we have elections," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance, said.
"They're a bit sanguine, saying if the Socialists win it may not make that much difference and anyway Labour in the U.K. has been very popular with markets," he said.
Analysts said while polls should always be treated with caution and even a consensus among polls may not predict the outcome, faith in a win for the ruling coalition was unwise.

"I think markets are being a bit silly. They're just looking at the bare headlines on the polls and are taking it to mean the government is going to get in. I don't think it's at all clear," Phyllis Reed, bond analyst at BZW in London, said.
"All hell could break loose, maybe not to the same degree as in the past...but there's still a policy dilemma that markets could challenge," Reed said.

She said while the long-end of the bond market was well protected by domestic buy-and-hold investors the two-year spread between French and German bonds could gape to 50 basis points from 17 now and the franc could come under limited pressure.
"This is not a Tony Blair style Socialism...what the Socialists are proposing is to turn around and walk backwards," Paul Horne at Smith Barney in Paris said.
Equity analysts said investors' laid-back attitude towards the election, combined with a strong U.S. market and excess liquidity among equity investors was helping support the market.
"There are very few investors who have made a detailed analysis," Olivier Davanne, at Goldman Sachs, said.
The CAC-40 share index was buoyed by the U.S. stock market last week and it was trading around 2,650 compared with 2,640 when the election jitters hit, but some were becoming cautious.

"The international environment is favourable. But in France, the elections are a close run and therefore a consolidation has to take place. There is no reason for the Bourse to rise much," a fund manager said.

The main concern is that a Socialist-led government could increase tension in Europe. While they are in favour of a single currency their refusal to countenance more fiscal austerity to hit tough Maastricht goals could cause problems with Germany.

Some said the French markets could actually be right but for the wrong reasons - not because the centre-right are assured victory but because the Socialists may not ultimately have much impact on European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"I'm not sure they can do much unless there's a new government in Germany but that couldn't happen until late next year," Brossard said. "The Socialists are just asking for what (President) Chirac asked for initially. He didn't succeed with a large majority, I'm not sure the Socialists could do much more."

Still, analysts said the cloud hanging over government policy with a centre-right president and a pro-EMU Socialist party relying on support from anti-Maastricht Communists would make markets nervous initially.

Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch, said the pro-EMU Socialist policy justified some complacency but a victory would provide a short-term shock and that anyway under any government the chances were growing that the euro may not be that strong.

"I still hold that under any sort of French government buy the dollar. The French are pushing for a euro which represents the economic environment (in Europe)...and this would be different to the environment under the Bundesbank," she said.
Implied three-month interest rates have climbed 40 basis points since the election was called and some said another 50 basis point rise was not out of the question.

For now the French franc has remained relatively unfazed by polls this week showing the Socialists virtually neck and neck with the centre-right and it has been stuck within a two-pfennig range against the mark throughout 1997.
"The French franc has really done nothing. It's only had a sneeze, it hasn't got a cold and it hasn't even reached for the Kleenex box yet," Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais said.
